title: Video projector (lamp, LED or laser): safe teardown
summary: Get the glass projection lens, mirrors and condenser lenses, the fans and blowers, heat sinks, the colour wheel motor, speakers and the power supply out of a video projector. Lamp projectors hold a mercury lamp under very high pressure that runs hot and can burst, fed by a driver that makes kilovolts to start it; laser projectors can hold a high-power laser; portable ones hold a lithium battery.

steps.text: Unplug it, pull out every other cable and keep the plug where you can see it. If it is ceiling-mounted or hard-wired, switch its breaker off and tag it instead (see the next step), and switch off any UPS or other backup supply that feeds it. If it has been on, let it cool for at least an hour before you touch the lamp (Epson EX9200 lamp FAQ).
steps.warn: Never switch a projector on with any cover off. Opening it exposes dangerous voltages (Epson CO-FH02 safety), and on laser models a high-power laser (Epson W70/W75 laser safety).

steps.text: Ceiling-mounted or hard-wired: with the breaker off and tagged, prove its supply wires dead with a meter you have checked on a known source, and check the meter again after (see safety_mains_isolation). Use a non-metal ladder, keep three points of contact, and have a helper who takes the weight before the last fixing comes out. Hand it down: never carry it down the ladder. Take it down before you open any cover.

Battery projectors (pocket and portable models): before you open anything, look and feel for swelling, heat or a sweet smell. If you find any, stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium. Don't charge it to see if it works unless it sits on stone or a metal tray where you can watch it, and unplug it if it gets warm.
Find out what makes its light. A spec label or manual saying laser, or a laser warning label, means a laser model. LED means LED. A separate lamp cover held by screws usually means a mercury lamp.
steps.warn: On a laser model, take only the case, boards, fans, speakers and battery. Leave the light engine closed. Epson says not to take its projector apart, as it contains a high-power laser component and serious injury could result (Epson W70/W75 laser safety).

steps.text: Lamp models: put on gloves and safety glasses. Undo the lamp cover screws, loosen the lamp's captive screws and lift the lamp module out by its handle only (iFixit Mitsubishi EX320U). Don't touch its glass (Epson EX9200 lamp FAQ). Leave the bulb in its cage and put the whole module into a strong box or a jar with a lid, labelled MERCURY.
steps.warn: Lamps hold mercury under high pressure: Philips UHP lamps run at 200–250 bar (Signify UHP leaflet). Finger grease on the glass can shorten its life and may make it burst (iFixit Mitsubishi EX320U).

steps.text: If the lamp glass is broken or rattles: everyone leaves the room, open the windows and stay out for at least 15 minutes. Don't vacuum or sweep. Pick up glass and silver beads with stiff card and sticky tape into a glass jar with a lid, and label it. Glass in the eyes or mouth needs a doctor (Epson CO-FH02 safety).

Undo the case screws: bits vary. The 3M SCP176 case is mostly #1 Phillips (its tool list names a T10 security bit, but the one T10 screw is on the lamp: iFixit 3M SCP176), and the Mitsubishi EX320U needs Pozidriv (iFixit Mitsubishi EX320U). Lift the top cover, photograph everything, and touch nothing inside yet: no boards, no connectors, no wires.
Battery models: with a plastic tool, unplug the battery connector from the main board and tape over its end. Leave the pack where it is for now.
steps.warn: Never put a metal blade or screwdriver near the cells or in a seam beside them.

steps.text: Wait at least 5 minutes since you unplugged it. Check your meter on a known source. Find the big capacitors on the power supply and the lamp driver, and any capacitor in the driver's igniter section (one Sony design charges a capacitor to make the start pulse: Sony US 6,686,704). Leave the high-voltage lead to the lamp and the pulse transformer alone. Discharge each with a resistor tool, measure DC volts across it, and check the meter on the known source again. Under 1 V is safe; clip a wire across each big one while you work (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: A projector's power-factor stage can make about 400 V DC for the lamp driver (Electronic Design TI projector power); a Sony patent gives 5–20 kV for the igniter (Sony US 6,686,704). One hand only, and never short a capacitor with a screwdriver.

steps.text: Unplug the connectors by their plugs, not their wires (iFixit Mitsubishi EX320U), and lift the power supply out as a whole board. Lift the lamp driver out only if it is in your way: it is not worth keeping (see the notes). The Smart UF75 has two supplies, each held by four screws (iFixit Smart UF75).
Take the fans and blowers: unplug each one and pull it out of its rubber mounts (iFixit 3M SCP176). Then the main board, any infrared receivers, and the speakers.

Lamp and LED models: unscrew the optical engine and lift it out with the lens. On a laser model skip this step and the next. On DLP models, take out the colour wheel: two screws and a cable tie on the Smart UF75 (iFixit Smart UF75). The wheel is thin glass that breaks easily: don't squeeze or drop it. The Acer guide turns it out while holding the ribbon cable (iFixit Acer S1210).
steps.warn: Don't touch the mirrors' silvered faces: they scratch easily (iFixit Smart UF75).

steps.text: Lamp and LED models: take the projection lens and the condenser lenses out of the engine, and the mirrors only if they come out without force (the Smart UF75's mirror is riveted in and can't come out undamaged: iFixit Smart UF75). Wrap each in a soft cloth and store lenses covered.
steps.warn: A lens can focus sunlight hot enough to burn skin and start fires. Keep it covered when you're not using it.

steps.text: LED models: unplug and unscrew the LED modules with their heat sinks. On all models, take the heat sinks from the main chips. On lamp and LED models, take the heat sinks and heat pipes from the light source too; on a laser model leave them with the laser module.
Battery models: lift the pack out with plastic tools only. If it is wired in, cut one lead at a time and tape each end at once. Store it on a non-flammable surface.
steps.warn: Don't bend, puncture or pry the cells.

steps.text: Test the parts (see the notes) and label each one OK or BAD.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Projection lens, condensers and mirrors.** A multi-element glass lens makes a strong magnifier, a burning glass for starting fires in sun, or the optics for a simple slide or signal lamp. The Smart UF75's mirror is silvered on its front face and scratches easily (iFixit Smart UF75): front-silvered mirrors are good for signalling, but clean them only by blowing dust off.
- **Fans and blowers.** Small low-voltage fans that cool electronics, dry food or blow air into a small stove. Read the voltage on each label.
- **Colour wheel motor (DLP models).** A small, fast motor; the wheel bearing can't be oiled and should spin freely when flicked (iFixit Acer S1210). It needs its own driver, so it is mostly a spare.
- **Heat sinks and heat pipes.** For LED lamps, power transistors and solar charge controllers.
- **LEDs (LED models).** The ViewSonic M1X uses RGB LEDs (ViewSonic M1X specifications). Run them only from a current-limited LED driver, never straight from a battery.
- **Battery (portable models).** The ViewSonic M1X has three 3.7 V, 3,930 mAh cells (ViewSonic M1X specifications); the Anker Nebula Capsule 3 Laser has a 52 Wh built-in battery (Anker Capsule 3 Laser). Test each cell before reuse (see test_lithium_cell and safety_swollen_lithium).
- **Adapter (portable models).** The M1X adapter gives 19 V, 3.26 A (ViewSonic M1X specifications); the Capsule 3 Laser charges from USB-C power delivery at 20 V, 2.25 A (Anker Capsule 3 Laser). Good for other gear that takes the same voltage and no more current.
- **Speakers and infrared receivers.** The M1X has two 3 W speakers (ViewSonic M1X specifications).
- **Power supply board.** Spares, and the low-voltage outputs printed on the board.

## Testing what you got out

- **Fans.** Feed the label voltage from a bench supply (30 V or less), red to plus. It should spin smoothly and quietly.
- **Lenses.** In sunshine, a good lens gives a small, sharp, bright spot on paper. Do this outdoors, on bare ground, with water to hand.
- **Lithium cells.** See test_lithium_cell. Charge only on stone or a tray, watched, and unplug if warm.
- **Adapters.** Measure the output: within about 5% of the label is good.

## Variations

- **Lamp projectors (DLP).** The 3M SCP176 uses an Osram P-VIP 180–230 W lamp, and the iFixit teardown warns of broken glass and mercury and says to discharge the power supply (iFixit 3M SCP176). In a DLP projector a colour wheel spins in front of the lamp and lights the chip with each colour in turn (iFixit Mitsubishi EX320U); the Smart UF75's chip has 1024 × 768 mirrors (iFixit Smart UF75).
- **The UHP lamp.** Its only light-making fill is mercury, at more than 200 bar (Philips UHP paper); Signify gives 200–250 bar and extremely high temperatures, and says the lamps must be handled with care (Signify UHP leaflet). Without an ignition aid it needs about 20 kV to start; with Philips' built-in UV ignition aid, about 5 kV. Once lit, it needs a few hundred volts and then under 100 V (Philips UHP paper). Epson says shock, vibration or very long use can make a lamp break, and that a bursting lamp throws out gas and glass (Epson CO-FH02 safety).
- **Laser projectors.** The Epson W70/W75 is a Class 1 laser product as a whole, with a high-power laser part inside; Epson says don't take it apart, even for disposal. Its page also carries a Risk Group 2 mark (IEC 62471-5) and says not to stare into the beam, so Class 1 is not a reason to look into the lens (Epson W70/W75 laser safety). The Anker Nebula Capsule 3 Laser lists a laser light source (Anker Capsule 3 Laser).
- **LED projectors.** The ViewSonic M1X uses RGB LEDs and runs from three built-in cells or a 19 V adapter (ViewSonic M1X specifications).

## What to leave

- **The lamp module.** Keep it whole and sealed in a labelled jar or box, away from heat, outdoors or in a shed rather than where people sleep; it holds mercury under pressure, and Epson says shock or vibration can break it (Epson CO-FH02 safety). If a lamp has broken, glass may be loose inside its chamber (Epson EX9200 lamp FAQ). Never try to light a salvaged lamp.
- **The laser module** of a laser projector (Epson W70/W75 laser safety).
- **The lamp driver (ballast) board.** A TI design article puts its supply at a regulated 400 V DC (Electronic Design TI projector power), and a Sony patent describes a 300–400 V DC supply and a 5–20 kV start pulse (Sony US 6,686,704). Don't keep it: it is no use without its own lamp.
- **The DLP chip, LCD panels and main board,** unless you are repairing the same model.
